clinicalPearls: Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan parasite of humans and the only ciliate that causes human disease
Pigs are the principal reservoir, and infection follows ingestion of cysts in food or water contaminated by porcine faeces, so it clusters where people live in close contact with pigs
Most infections are asymptomatic, but invasive disease produces a colitis resembling amoebic dysentery with abdominal pain, tenesmus and bloody, mucoid diarrhoea
The trophozoite is large, ciliated and rapidly motile on a fresh wet stool preparation, with a characteristic macronucleus, making it recognisable microscopically
Colonic ulceration mirrors that of amoebiasis and can lead to perforation; extraintestinal spread is rare but described
Malnutrition, alcoholism and immunosuppression predispose to symptomatic and severe disease
Tetracycline is the usual first-line treatment, with metronidazole as an effective alternative
reference.pathophysiology: Balantidium coli exists as a large motile trophozoite and a resistant cyst that transmits infection. After cysts are ingested, excystation in the small intestine releases trophozoites that colonise the large bowel. Secreting proteolytic enzymes such as hyaluronidase, the trophozoites can invade the colonic mucosa, producing flask-shaped ulcers closely resembling those of amoebic colitis with surrounding inflammation and haemorrhage. Tissue invasion drives the dysenteric illness, and in severe cases confluent ulceration may cause perforation and peritonitis. Host factors such as malnutrition, achlorhydria and immunosuppression favour invasion and more severe disease.
additionalInvestigations: Fresh stool wet-mount microscopy for large motile ciliated trophozoites
Stool concentration methods to detect cysts
Repeated stool examination because shedding is intermittent
Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy of ulcer edges in invasive disease
Full blood count and markers of inflammation and dehydration
Assessment of nutritional and immune status
redFlags: Severe bloody dysentery with dehydration and haemodynamic compromise
Signs of colonic perforation or peritonitis
Fulminant colitis in a malnourished or immunosuppressed patient
Failure to respond to appropriate therapy
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic carriage and mild disease resolve well with treatment; invasive colitis carries a more serious outlook, and fulminant or perforating disease, particularly in debilitated hosts, can be fatal.
pitfalls: Mistaking invasive balantidial colitis for amoebiasis and not identifying the ciliate
Relying on a single stool sample despite intermittent trophozoite and cyst shedding
Overlooking the epidemiological clue of pig contact
Underestimating severity in malnourished or immunosuppressed patients
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with antiparasitic therapy, using a tetracycline such as doxycycline first-line, with metronidazole or iodoquinol as alternatives
Provide supportive care with rehydration and correction of electrolyte disturbance in dysenteric illness
Monitor for and surgically manage complications of invasive colitis such as perforation and peritonitis
Address predisposing factors by treating malnutrition and assessing and managing immunosuppression
Improve sanitation and reduce contact with pig faeces, screening or treating close contacts where indicated
Confirm parasitological clearance with follow-up stool examination given intermittent shedding
